original_interpretation: TSMC's October 2021 blog gave OIP as 16 EDA, 6 Cloud, 37 IP, 21 DCA and 8 VCA partners.
evidence_found: "As the industry's most comprehensive ecosystem, TSMC's OIP alliance currently consists of 16 EDA partners, six Cloud partners, 37 IP partners, 21 design center alliance (DCA) partners, and eight value chain aggregator (VCA) partners." (TSMC blog by Suk Lee, 25 Oct 2021, para. 6)
notes: All five counts match. Historical snapshot (Oct 2021), correctly dated in the claim. Newer counts: 2024 AR (CLM-1469) and 2025 AR (new claim in this batch: 13 EDA, 7 Cloud, 37 IP, 29 DCA, 8 VCA, 23 3DFabric).

original_interpretation: TSMC's 2024 annual report gives OIP participants as 16 EDA, 7 Cloud, 40 IP, 29 design center alliance and 8 value chain aggregator partners, plus 23 3DFabric Alliance partners.
evidence_found: "Participants consisting of 16 EDA partners seven Cloud partners ... 40 IP partners ... 29 design center alliance (DCA) partners ... eight value chain aggregator (VCA) partners ... and 23 partners in the new TSMC 3DFabric® Alliance" (TSMC 2024 Annual Report, e-book page 113; printed page 111)
notes: All six counts match the 2024 annual report as stated. Newer data exists: TSMC 2025 Annual Report s.5.2.3 gives 13 EDA, seven Cloud, 37 IP, 29 DCA, eight VCA and 23 3DFabric partners. Added as a new claim with supersedes: CLM-1469 (the 2024-report statement itself stays true as a historical figure). E-book page 113 = printed p.111.

original_interpretation: TSMC appointed a Chief Information Security Officer in 2022 and in 2024 renamed its corporate information security organisation Global Security Management; it says it is committed to confidentiality protection for customers.
evidence_found: "TSMC is committed to information security and confidentiality protection for its customers shareholders and partners ... In 2022 ... TSMC appointed J K Lin ... to take on the addition role of Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) ... In 2024 ... the organization was renamed Global Security Management (GSM)" (2024 AR, e-book p.113, s.5.5.1)
notes: Matches. Detail: J K Lin took the CISO role in addition to his SVP job; from 2025 Cliff Hou (SVP and Deputy Co-COO) became CISO. The 'committed to confidentiality' part is TSMC describing itself (reported claim inside a fact record).

original_interpretation: TSMC's CyberShuttle multi-project wafer service lets multiple designs share a multi-project mask set, covering processes from 0.5 um to A14 with up to 10 shuttles a month, and TSMC claims it cuts prototyping cost by up to 90%.
evidence_found: "significantly reduces non-recurring engineering (NRE) costs across the broadest technology range (from 0.5μm to A14), with the most frequent launch schedule (up to 10 shuttles per month)"; "enabling multiple designs to share tooling costs through a multi-project mask set"; "Slashes prototyping cost by up to 90%" (TSMC CyberShuttle page)
notes: All elements match. The 90% cost cut is TSMC marketing with no baseline given; reported_claim is the right type.

original_interpretation: Intel Foundry's Accelerator Ecosystem Alliance programme comprises IP, EDA, Design Services, Cloud, USMAG (US military, aerospace and government), Value Chain and Chiplet alliances.
evidence_found: Page lists headings "IP Alliance", "EDA Alliance", "Design Services Alliance", "Cloud Alliance", "USMAG Alliance" ("United States Military, Aerospace, and Government Alliance enables national security and government applications"), "Value Chain Alliance", "Chiplet Alliance" (Intel Foundry Accelerator page)
notes: Seven alliances listed as claimed. Current web page; undated.

original_interpretation: Intel says its EDA Alliance partners get early access to Intel process technologies so they can co-optimise tools and flows.
evidence_found: "Our EDA Alliance partners get early access to Intel's process technologies, allowing these partners to co-optimize tools and flows to best realize Intel's technology capabilities." (EDA Alliance page, para. 2)
notes: Exact wording found. Intel marketing; reported_claim is correct.

original_interpretation: Intel Foundry Services launched the Accelerator ecosystem alliance in February 2022 with 17 founding partners, including Ansys, Cadence, Siemens EDA and Synopsys in its EDA Alliance.
evidence_found: "With today's comprehensive launch of the IFS Accelerator – including 17 founding partner companies"; "EDA Alliance: Ansys, Cadence, Siemens EDA, Synopsys" (Intel press release, 7 Feb 2022)
notes: Matches. Caveats: the release says IFS launched Accelerator's 'preliminary phase in September 2021' (automotive IP), so February 2022 was the full launch. Counting the names listed (EDA 4, IP 11, Design Services 3; Cadence and Synopsys in two groups) gives 16 unique companies, not 17; the release does not explain the gap.

original_interpretation: Intel described EDA tools, IP and design services as 'the foundation of customer interaction with a foundry manufacturing partner'.
evidence_found: "Why It's Important: These three capabilities are the foundation of customer interaction with a foundry manufacturing partner." (Intel press release, 7 Feb 2022; the 'three capabilities' are EDA tools, IP and design services listed just before)
notes: Exact quote found.

original_interpretation: Intel released the Intel 18A PDK 1.0 in July 2024; its EDA and IP partners then updated their tools and flows so external foundry customers could begin final production designs, with the first external 18A tape-out expected in the first half of 2025.
evidence_found: "In July, Intel released the 18A Process Design Kit (PDK) 1.0"; "Electronic design automation (EDA) and intellectual property (IP) partners are updating their offerings to enable customers to begin their final production designs"; "the first external customer is expected to tape out on Intel 18A in the first half of next year" (Intel newsroom, 6 Aug 2024)
notes: Matches. The tape-out date is Intel's Aug 2024 forecast, and the claim words it as an expectation; whether that tape-out happened was not checked. The URL now redirects to intel.com/content/www/us/en/newsroom/news/intel-foundry-achieves-major-milestones.html.

original_interpretation: Siemens announced in April 2025 that TSMC certified its Calibre nmDRC, nmLVS, PERC and YieldEnhancer signoff tools for TSMC N2P and A16, and that seven Siemens signoff flows were certified to run on AWS cloud.
evidence_found: "Calibre® DRC software, Calibre® LVS software, Calibre® PERC, and Calibre® YieldEnhancer™ software with SmartFill technology are certified for the TSMC's advanced N2P and A16 processes"; "Siemens EDA and TSMC have successfully certified seven sign-off production flows on cloud ... verified to run ... on the AWS Cloud." (Siemens press release, 24 Apr 2025)
notes: Date (April 24, 2025) and content confirmed. The seven cloud flows include Solido SPICE, AFS and mPower as well as Calibre tools. Siemens is announcing this itself (reported_claim).

original_interpretation: Siemens describes mask data preparation after tape-out as a chain of resolution enhancement (OPC, phase-shift, scattering bars), geometry processing, mask rule checking and conversion ('fracture') of GDSII/OASIS into mask-writer formats.
evidence_found: "enabling a seamless continuation of the data manipulations required for resolution enhancement techniques (RET)—such as phase shift mask (PSM), scattering bars (SB) and optical and process correction (OPC)—to the mask data format conversion in one batch run"; "Efficient, direct conversion of GDSII and OASIS input files into mask writer formats"; MRC and FRACTURE listed (Calibre MDP fact sheet p.1-2)
correction: Siemens presents RET (OPC, PSM, scattering bars) as the step before mask data preparation, which its integrated flow connects to; MDP itself covers geometry processing, MRC/MPC and fracture.
notes: Geometry processing, mask rule checking (MRC) and fracture of GDSII/OASIS into writer formats are confirmed. Caveat: the sheet treats RET (OPC/PSM/SB) as the upstream step that MDP 'seamlessly continues' from ('extension of tapeout verification and RET into mask data generation'), not as part of MDP itself. The sheet is dated 2019 but carries code '83159-C1 06/2006', so the content is old.

original_interpretation: Siemens states that both tape-out groups (on the design/fab side) and mask makers run mask data preparation and face growing data volumes and compute times.
evidence_found: "Tape-out groups and mask makers are facing a tremendous growth in data volumes and computing times driven by the deployment of ever larger designs and ever more-intense resolution enhancement techniques, such as OPC, PSM and scatter-bars" (Calibre MDP fact sheet p.2, 'Calibre mask data preparation')
correction: Source says tape-out groups and mask makers both face growing MDP data volumes/compute times; it does not explicitly state that both perform MDP.
notes: The quote is exact. The sheet says both groups face growing data volumes and compute times. That both run mask data preparation is only implied by the section heading; the sheet does not say it. '(on the design/fab side)' is the researcher's own gloss.

original_interpretation: Synopsys's mask data preparation product performs mask fracture, mask error correction, mask rule checking and job deck viewing/editing, and supports MEBES, laser-write, variable-shaped-beam and multibeam writer formats.
evidence_found: "MDP provides a comprehensive solution that performs mask fracture, mask error correction, mask rule checking, and a graphical and job view debugging platform."; "supports all major mask writer formats for MEBES, Laser Write, Variable Shaped Beam (VSB), and Multibeam Mask Writers (MBMW)"; "Jobdeck graphical viewing and editing" (Synopsys MDP datasheet, 04/14/26)
notes: All elements match. Vendor datasheet (reported_claim).

original_interpretation: A commercial mask-data viewer (Nippon Control System neoEBV) lists support for GDSII, OASIS, OASIS.MASK, OASIS.CL (SEMI P49), MEBES, JEOL, VSB and other writer formats, each with its own job deck format (e.g. MALY for OASIS.MASK, JB for MEBES).
evidence_found: Table 'Displayable Pattern File Format': "OASIS.MASK | SEMI P44-1105, SEMI P44-0709 P44-1216 | Maly (SEMI P45-0306N, SEMI P45-1218)"; "MEBES | | JB, Extended MEBES Jobdeck"; "OASIS.CL (SEMI P49) | SEMI P49-0823"; "JEOL | | JDK, JDF"; "VSB | | MDS"; GDSII and OASIS rows have no jobdeck (neoEBV Supported Formats, modified 16 Apr 2026)
correction: Only some formats have a jobdeck format in the table (e.g. MALY for OASIS.MASK, JB for MEBES, JDK/JDF for JEOL, MDS for VSB/MBF); GDSII, OASIS and OASIS.CL have none.
notes: All formats and the MALY/JB examples are confirmed. 'Each with its own job deck format' overgeneralises: GDSII, OASIS, OASIS.CL, GERBER, MBW and P44MultiFile have no jobdeck in the table, and VSB and MBF share MDS.

original_interpretation: Photronics says its CyberMask service uses SEMI P10 data structures and automates mask front-end functions including order entry, data fracture, job decking and measurement file generation.
evidence_found: "CyberMask leverages Semi P10 data specifications – industry-standard data structures ..."; "Front-end functions automated by CyberMask include: Order entry, Data fracture, Job decking, Measure file generation, Production control flagging" (Photronics On-Line Data Services page)
notes: Matches. Photronics is describing its own service (reported_claim).

original_interpretation: Photronics claims CyberMask reduces mask front-end process time by more than 75% and offers a password-protected extranet (MaskLink) for customers to check mask order status.
evidence_found: "CyberMask helps reduce process time by more than 75%, while simultaneously reducing the risk of human error."; "an innovative, password-protected extranet where you can check your mask product status online via MaskLink™" (Photronics On-Line Data Services page)
notes: Matches. The 75% figure is marketing with no baseline or date given; the page is undated.

original_interpretation: Cadence states that it works with semiconductor ecosystem partners to develop foundry PDKs so that its core EDA products meet manufacturing sign-off requirements.
evidence_found: "We work closely with leading semiconductor ecosystem partners to develop foundry process design kits (“PDKs”) to ensure our core EDA products and solutions meet manufacturing sign-off requirements." (Cadence FY2025 10-K, Item 1, Core EDA)
notes: Exact. This is a filing, but the statement is Cadence describing its own work (close to a reported_claim).

original_interpretation: Cadence describes physical verification and signoff - design rule checking (DRC) and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) - as the checks that ensure manufacturing compliance of a layout.
evidence_found: "comprehensive physical verification and signoff flows, including design rule checking (“DRC”) and layout-versus-schematic (“LVS”) verification, ensure manufacturing compliance." (Cadence FY2025 10-K, Item 1, Custom IC Design and Simulation)
notes: Exact.

original_interpretation: Cadence licenses software mainly as time-based licences of generally two to three years with no rights to return; some include rights to 'remix' among delivered products.
evidence_found: "We primarily license our software using time-based licenses ... throughout the entire term of the arrangement, which is generally two to three years, with no rights to return. In addition, certain time-based license arrangements include the right for the customer to remix among the products delivered at the outset of the arrangement" (FY2025 10-K, Product Arrangements)
notes: Exact. Remix rights also cover 'unspecified additional products that become commercially available during the term'.

original_interpretation: Cadence licenses design IP under non-exclusive licences granting usage rights for specific designs, and collects royalties on some IP as customers ship products containing it.
evidence_found: "We generally license our design IP under nonexclusive license agreements that provide usage rights for specific designs ... for certain IP license agreements, we collect royalties as our customers ship their product that includes our IP" (FY2025 10-K, Product Arrangements)
notes: Exact.

original_interpretation: Cadence distributes its software and documentation to customers primarily by secure electronic delivery.
evidence_found: "Software and documentation are primarily distributed to customers by secure electronic delivery." (FY2025 10-K, Hardware Manufacturing and Software Distribution)
notes: Exact.

original_interpretation: Cadence says it supports third-party design tools and IP through its Cadence Connections programme and through industry groups including the Silicon Integration Initiative (Si2) and Accellera.
evidence_found: "We support the use of third-party design products and design IP through our Cadence Connections® program and through our participation in industry groups such as the Silicon Integration Initiative and Accellera System Initiative." (FY2025 10-K, Competition)
notes: Exact. The 10-K writes 'Accellera System Initiative'; the body is usually called Accellera Systems Initiative.

original_interpretation: Cadence notes trade rules may require authorisation before some non-US-person employees can perform duties that involve export, reexport or transfer of export-controlled technology.
evidence_found: "Future trade regulations may also impact our ability to transact business ... and may restrict certain non-U.S. person employees from performing their duties at Cadence without first obtaining appropriate authorization if their duties involve an export, reexport, or transfer of export-controlled technology." (FY2025 10-K, Government Regulations - Trade)
notes: Exact. This is a forward-looking risk statement, and the claim's 'may' keeps that sense.

original_interpretation: Cadence's FY2025 10-K notes BIS's 29 September 2025 interim final rule extending Entity List and Military End-User restrictions to entities 50% or more owned by listed parties, and its one-year suspension published 11 November 2025, set to expire 9 November 2026.
evidence_found: 10-K: "effective September 29, 2025, BIS issued an interim final rule that extended the export restrictions ... to entities that are 50% or more owned by one or more of such entities. However, on November 11, 2025, BIS published a one-year suspension of the new rule that is currently set to expire on November 9, 2026, absent a future extension." FR 2025-19846: published 11/12/2025; IFR stayed until November 9, 2026.
correction: As of 2026-09-30 the 9 Nov 2026 expiry is likely to move: the US-China truce extension to 10 Jan 2027 (announced 24 Sep 2026) is expected to extend the suspension, but BIS had not yet formalised it. The FR publication date is 12 Nov 2025, not 11 Nov.
notes: The 10-K says what the claim says. Two caveats: (1) the Federal Register shows the suspension published on 12 Nov 2025 and effective 10 Nov 2025, while the 10-K says 11 Nov (likely public-inspection timing); (2) on 24 Sep 2026 Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the US-China truce would run to 10 Jan 2027. Crowell & Moring (30 Sep 2026) says this pushes back the affiliates rule's return, but no Federal Register notice had been published as of that date. New claims added.

original_interpretation: On 23 May 2025 BIS informed Cadence that a licence was required to export, re-export or transfer in-country EDA software and technology classified ECCN 3D991 and 3E991 when a party was in China or was a Chinese military end user anywhere.
evidence_found: 8-K Item 8.01: "on May 23, 2025, the Bureau of Industry and Security (“BIS”) ... informed Cadence ... that a license was required for the export, re-export or in-country transfer of electronic design automation software and technology classified under ... ECCNs 3D991 and 3E991 ... when a party to the transaction is located in China or is a Chinese “military end user” wherever located." Same text in FY2025 10-K.
notes: Confirmed in both the 8-K (opened via web_extract; the browser was blocked by SEC's automated-tool wall) and the 10-K. The 10-K adds 'on the Military End-User List'.

original_interpretation: On 2 July 2025 BIS informed Cadence that the May 2025 EDA licence requirements were rescinded effective immediately.
evidence_found: "On July 2, 2025, BIS informed Cadence that the license requirements set forth in the May 23, 2025 letter from BIS were rescinded effective immediately." (Cadence 8-K, Item 8.01; same wording in FY2025 10-K)
notes: Exact.

original_interpretation: Synopsys reported receiving a BIS letter imposing China-related export restrictions on 29 May 2025, and a further BIS letter on 2 July 2025 rescinding them effective immediately.
evidence_found: "On July 2, 2025, Synopsys received a letter from the Bureau of Industry and Security of the U.S. Department of Commerce informing Synopsys that the export restrictions related to China, pursuant to a letter received on May 29, 2025, have now been rescinded, effective immediately." (Synopsys 8-K, Item 8.01)
notes: Exact. The 8-K does not describe what the May 29 letter restricted beyond 'export restrictions related to China'.

original_interpretation: In July 2025 Cadence agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to violate export controls for supplying EDA hardware, software and design IP to China's National University of Defense Technology (NUDT), on the Entity List since February 2015, via the alias Central South CAD Center.
evidence_found: "Cadence ... has agreed to plead guilty to resolve charges that Cadence committed criminal violations of export controls by selling EDA hardware, software, and semiconductor design intellectual property (IP) technology to ... (NUDT)"; NUDT "was added to ... the Entity List in February 2015"; "through Central South CAD Center (CSCC), an alias for NUDT" (DOJ, 28 Jul 2025)
notes: All elements confirmed. The conspiracy (Feb 2015 to Apr 2021) also covered Phytium Technology.

original_interpretation: Cadence admitted that NUDT personnel downloaded EDA software and IP from Cadence's download portals and that Cadence China staff installed EDA hardware on NUDT's Changsha campus.
evidence_found: "Cadence admitted that Cadence China employees installed EDA hardware on NUDT's Changsha, China, campus and that NUDT personnel downloaded EDA software and IP technology from Cadence's download portals while Cadence and Cadence China ... had knowledge that NUDT had been added to the Entity List." (DOJ press release, 28 Jul 2025)
notes: Exact.

original_interpretation: Cadence's coordinated DOJ and BIS resolutions total more than US$140 million net: criminal penalties of nearly US$118 million and a BIS civil penalty of over US$95 million, with cross-crediting.
evidence_found: "agreed to plead guilty and pay criminal penalties of nearly $118 million"; BIS "Cadence has agreed to pay over $95 million in civil penalties"; "each agreeing to credit against their respective fines a portion of the payments"; "Cadence will pay aggregate net criminal and civil penalties and forfeiture totaling more than $140 million." (DOJ, 28 Jul 2025)
notes: Confirmed. BIS's release adds that the DOJ agreement 'includes $45 million in forfeitures', and the BIS order sets the civil penalty at exactly $95,312,000. The metric (USD 140m lower bound) is correct.

original_interpretation: In its BIS settlement Cadence admitted 56 EAR violations between September 2015 and September 2020 for EDA hardware, software and design technology worth US$45,305,317.41 sold to NUDT through the CSCC alias.
evidence_found: "Cadence admitted to 56 violations of the EAR between September 2015 and September 2020, for selling EDA products to NUDT through an alias, Central South CAD Center (CSCC). Cadence exported EDA hardware and software, and semiconductor design technology, valued at $45,305,317.41" (BIS press release, 28 Jul 2025)
notes: Exact. The BIS final order confirms 56 charges (1-56) totalling about $45,305,317.41. These 56 are a subset of the 61 violations admitted overall (see new claim on the 61-charge breakdown).

original_interpretation: BIS says that after freezing sales to the CSCC account, Cadence assigned the CSCC contracts to Phytium, another NUDT-linked company, producing two further violations between about November 2020 and February 2021.
evidence_found: "Cadence froze sales to the CSCC account ... Cadence then agreed to assign its contracts with CSCC to Phytium, another company linked to NUDT"; "Cadence's transfer of EDA software and semiconductor design technology that had been previously exported to CSCC resulted in two more violations between approximately November 2020 and February 2021." (BIS press release)
notes: Confirmed. The order shows charge 57 is the actual software/IP transfer (about 11 Nov 2020 to 1 Feb 2021) and charge 58 is an attempted hardware transfer (about 1 Nov 2020 to 1 Feb 2021) that was never completed.

original_interpretation: The BIS settlement requires Cadence to undergo two independent third-party audits of its export compliance programme, including its Shanghai subsidiary, through 2028.
evidence_found: BIS Order, THIRD: "Cadence shall complete two (2) internal audits of its export controls compliance program, including but not limited to its oversight over export controls compliance by Cadence China"; first covers 12 months from 1 Sep 2025, report due 1 Mar 2027; second from 1 Sep 2026, report due 1 Mar 2028. No 'independent'/'third-party' wording in the 59-page order.
correction: The BIS order requires two internal audits (no independent or third-party requirement stated), covering Cadence's export compliance including oversight of Cadence China; audit periods start 1 Sep 2025 and 1 Sep 2026, with reports due 1 Mar 2027 and 1 Mar 2028.
notes: DLA Piper's summary does say 'third-party internal audits' and 'independent internal audits'. The primary BIS order and settlement agreement require two internal audits and never say 'independent' or 'third-party' (full-text search of the PDF). Two audits, Cadence China coverage and the 2028 end are confirmed. A corrected claim citing the order has been added.

original_interpretation: DLA Piper's summary of the Cadence resolution states that Cadence admitted 61 EAR violations in its civil settlement with BIS and agreed a US$95,312,000 civil penalty, half payable within 30 days and the rest suspended pending the DOJ fine.
evidence_found: DLA Piper: "Cadence also admitted to 61 violations of the EAR pursuant to a civil resolution with BIS, under which Cadence consented to: A USD95,312,000 civil penalty, with USD47,656,000 payable within 30 days, and the balance suspended pending payment of the DOJ fine". BIS Order: "alleges that Respondent committed 61 violations"; "civil penalty in the amount of $95,312,000 ... $47,656,000 within 30 days".
notes: DLA Piper's summary is accurate, and the primary BIS order confirms 61 violations and the payment terms. 61 = 56 CSCC sales/loans + 2 Phytium transfer charges + 3 charges for downloads by Entity-Listed Mikron, Huawei and SMIC. This settles CON-0050 (updated in this batch).
